<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader||ALGEBRAIC FORMS|631}}</noinclude>we find

{{block center|<math>\left(\frac{d}{d\text{X}}, \frac{d}{d\text{Y}}, \frac{d}{d\text{Z}}, \dots\right) = \begin{matrix}(\lambda_1, & \lambda_2, & \lambda_3, & \dots) \\ \left|\begin{matrix}\mu_1, & \mu_2, & \mu_3, & \dots \\ \nu_1, & \nu_2, & \nu_3, & \dots \\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot\end{matrix}\right|\end{matrix} \left(\frac{d}{dx}, \frac{d}{dy}, \frac{d}{dz}, \dots\right).</math>}}

Observe the notation, which is that introduced by Cayley into the theory of matrices which he himself created.

Just as cogrediency leads to a theory of covariants, so contragrediency leads to a theory of contravariants. If <math>u</math>, a quantic in <math>x</math>, <math>y</math>, <math>z</math>, ..., be expressed in terms of new variables <math>\text{X}</math>, <math>\text{Y}</math>, <math>\text{Z}</math> ...; and if <math>\xi</math>, <math>\eta</math>, <math>\zeta</math>, ..., be quantities contragredient to <math>x</math>, <math>y</math>, <math>z</math>, ...; there are found to exist functions of <math>\xi</math>, <math>\eta</math>, <math>\zeta</math>, ..., and of the coefficients in <math>u</math>, which need, at most, be multiplied by powers of the modulus to be made equal to the same functions of <math>\Xi</math>, <math>\text{H}</math>, <math>\text{Z}</math>, ... of the transformed coefficients of <math>u</math>; such functions are called ''contravariants'' of <math>u</math>. There also exist functions, which involve both sets of variables as well as the coefficients of <math>u</math>, possessing a like property; such have been termed ''mixed concomitants'', and they, like contravariants, may appertain as well to a system of forms as to a single form.

As between the original and transformed quantic we have the umbral relations

{{block center|<math>\text{A}_1 = \lambda_1 a_1 + \lambda_2 a_2,\ \text{A}_2 = \mu_1 a_1 + \mu_2 a_2,</math>}}

and for a second form

{{block center|<math>\text{B}_1 = \lambda_1 b_1 + \lambda_2 b_2;\ \text{B}_2 = \mu_1 b_1 + \mu_2 b_2.</math>}}

The original forms are <math>a^n_x</math>, <math>b^n_x</math>, and we may regard them ''either'' as ''different'' forms ''or'' as equivalent representations of the ''same'' form. In other words, <math>\text{B}</math>, <math>b</math> may be regarded as different or alternative symbols to <math>\text{A}</math>, <math>a</math>. In either case

{{block center|<math>(\text{AB}) = \text{A}_1\text{B}_2 - \text{A}_2\text{B}_1 = (\lambda\mu)(ab);</math>}} and, from the definition, <math>(ab)</math> possesses the invariant property. We cannot, however, say that it is an invariant unless it is expressible in terms of the real coefficients. Since <math>(ab) = a_1b_2 - a_2b_1</math>, that this may be the case each form must be linear; and if the forms be different <math>(ab)</math> is an invariant (simultaneous) of the two forms, its real expression being <math>\bar{a}_0\bar{b}_1 - \bar{a}_1\bar{b}_0</math>. This will be recognized as the resultant of the two linear forms. If the two linear forms be identical, the umbral sets <math>a_1</math>, <math>a_2</math>; <math>b_1</math>, <math>b_2</math> are alternative, are ultimately put equal to one another and <math>(ab)</math> vanishes. A single linear form has, in fact, no invariant. When either of the forms is of an order higher than the first <math>(ab)</math>, as not being expressible in terms of the actual coefficients of the forms, is not an invariant and has no significance. Introducing now other sets of symbols <math>\text{C}</math>, <math>\text{D}</math>, ...; <math>c</math>, <math>d</math>, ... we may write
{{block center|<math>(\text{AB})^i(\text{AC})^j(\text{BC})^k\dots = (\lambda\mu)^{i+j+k+\dots}(ab)^i(ac)^j(bc)^k\dots,</math>}}
so that the symbolic product
{{block center|<math>(ab)^i(ac)^j(bc)^k\dots,</math>}}
possesses the invariant property. If the forms be all linear and different, the function is an invariant, viz. the <math>i^{th}</math> power of that appertaining to <math>a_x</math> and <math>b_x</math> multiplied by the <math>j^{th}</math> power of that appertaining to <math>a_x</math> and <math>c_x</math> multiplied by &c. If any two of the linear forms, say <math>p_x</math>, <math>q_x</math>, be supposed identical, any symbolic expression involving the factor <math>(pq)</math> is zero. Notice, therefore, that the symbolic product <math>(ab)^i(ac)^j(bc)^k\dots</math> may be always viewed as a simultaneous invariant of a number of different linear forms <math>a_x</math>, <math>b_x</math>, <math>c_x</math>, .... In order that <math>(ab)^i(ac)^j(bc)^k\dots</math> may be a simultaneous invariant of a number of different forms <math>a^{n_1}_x</math>, <math>b^{n_2}_x</math>, <math>c^{n_3}_x</math>,..., where <math>n_1</math>, <math>n_2</math>, <math>n_3</math>, ... may be the same or different, it is necessary that every product of umbrae which arises in the expansion of the symbolic product be of degree <math>n_1</math> in <math>a_1</math>, <math>a_2</math>; in the case of <math>b_1</math>, <math>b_2</math> of degree <math>n_2</math>; in the case of <math>c_1</math>, <math>c_2</math> of degree <math>n_3</math>; and so on. For these only will the symbolic product be replaceable by a linear function of products of real coefficients. Hence the condition is
{{block center|<math>i+j+\dots=n_1,</math>}}
{{block center|<math>i+k+\dots=n_2,</math>}}
{{block center|<math>j+k+\dots=n_3,</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\cdot\qquad\cdot\qquad\cdot\qquad\cdot</math>}}
If the forms <math>a^n_x</math>, <math>b^n_x</math>, <math>c^n_x</math>,...be identical the symbols are alternative, and provided that the form does not vanish it denotes an invariant of the single form <math>a^n_x</math>.

There may be a number of forms <math>a^n_x, b^n_x, c^n_x, \dots</math> and we may suppose such identities between the symbols that on the whole only two, three, or more of the sets of umbrae are not equivalent; we will then obtain invariants of two, three, or more sets of binary forms. The symbolic expression of a covariant is equally simple, because we see at once that since <math>\text{A}\xi</math>, <math>\text{B}\xi</math>, <math>\text{C}\xi</math>,... are equal to <math>a_x</math>, <math>b_x</math>, <math>c_x</math>, ... respectively, the linear forms <math>a_x</math>, <math>b_x</math>, <math>c_x</math>, ... possess the invariant property, and we may write
{{block center|<math>(\text{AB})^i(\text{AC})^j(\text{BC})^k\dots\text{A}^\rho_\xi\text{B}^\sigma_\xi\text{C}^\tau_\xi\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>=(\lambda\mu)^{i+j+k+\dots}(ab)^i(ac)^j(bc)^k\dots a^\rho_x b^\sigma_x c^\tau_x\dots,</math>}}
and assert that the symbolic product
{{block center|<math>(ab)^i(ac)^j(bc)^k\dots a^\rho_x b^\sigma_x c^\tau_x\dots</math>}} possesses the invariant property. It is always an invariant or covariant appertaining to a number of different linear forms, and as before it may vanish if two such linear forms be identical. In general it will be simultaneous covariant of the different forms <math>a_x^{n_1}</math>, <math>b_x^{n_2}</math>, <math>c_x^{n_3}</math>, ... if
{{block center|<math>i+j+\dots+\rho=n_1,</math>}}
{{block center|<math>i+k+\dots+\sigma=n_2,</math>}}
{{block center|<math>j+k+\dots+\tau=n_3,</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\cdot \qquad \cdot \qquad \cdot \qquad \cdot</math>}}

It will also be a covariant if the symbolic product be factorizable into portions each of which satisfies these conditions. If the forms be identical the sets of symbols are ultimately equated, and the form, provided it does not vanish, is a covariant of the form <math>a_x^n</math>.

The expression <math>(ab)^4</math> properly appertains to a quartic; for a quadratic it may also be written <math>(ab)^2 (cd)^2</math>, and would denote the square of the discriminant to a factor ''près''. For the quartic
{{block center|<math>(ab)^4=(a_1b_2-a_2b_1)^4=a_1^4b_2^4-4a_1^3a_2b_1b_2^3+6a_1^2a_2^2b_1^2b_2^2</math>}}
{{block center|<math>-4a_1a_2^3b_1^3b_2+a_2^4b_1^4=\bar{a}_0\bar{a}_4-4\bar{a}_1\bar{a}_3+6\bar{a}_2^2-4\bar{a}_1\bar{a}_3+\bar{a}_0\bar{a}_4</math>}}
{{block center|<math>=2(\bar{a}_0\bar{a}_4-4\bar{a}_1\bar{a}_3+3\bar{a}_2^2),</math>}}
one of the well-known invariants of the quartic.

For the cubic <math>(ab)^2a_xb_x</math> is a covariant because each symbol <math>a</math>, <math>b</math> occurs three times; we can first of all find its real expression as a simultaneous covariant of two cubics, and then, by supposing the two cubics to merge into identity, find the expression of the quadratic covariant, of the single cubic, commonly known as the Hessian.

By simple multiplication
{{block center|<math>(a_1^3b_1b_2^2-2a_1^2a_2b_1^2b_2+a_1a_2^2b_1^3)x_1^2</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+(a_1^3b_2^3-a_1a_2^2b_1^2b_2-a_1^2a_2b_1b_2^2+a_2^3b_1^3)x_1x_2</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+(a_1^2a_2b_2^3-2a_1a_2^2b_1b_2^2+a_2^3b_1^2b_2)x_2^2;</math>}}
and transforming to the real form, {{block center|<math>(a_0b_2-2a_1b_1+a_2b_0)x^2_1+(a_0b_3-a_1b_2-a_2b_1+a_3b_0)x_1x_2</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+(a_1b_3-2a_2b_2+a_3b_1)x^2_2,</math>}}
the simultaneous covariant; and now, putting <math>b=a</math>, we obtain twice the Hessian
{{block center|<math>(a_0a_2-a^2_1)x^2_1+(a_0a_3-a_1a_2)x_1x_2+(a_1a_3-a^2_2)x^2_2.</math>}}

It will be shown later that all invariants, single or simultaneous, are expressible in terms of symbolic products. The degree of the covariant in the coefficients is equal to the number of different symbols <math>a, b, c, \dots</math> that occur in the symbolic expression; the degree in the variables (''i.e.'' the order of the covariant) is <math>\rho+\sigma+\tau+\dots</math> and the weight<sup>1</sup> of the coefficient of the leading term <math>x^{\rho+\sigma+\tau+\dots}_1</math> is equal to <math>i+j+k+\dots</math>. It will be apparent that there are four numbers associated with a covariant, viz. the orders of the quantic and covariant, and the degree and weight of the leading coefficient; calling these <math>n</math>, <math>\epsilon</math>, <math>\theta</math>, <math>w</math> respectively we can see that they are not independent integers, but that they are invariably connected by a certain relation <math>n\theta-2w=\epsilon</math>. For, if <math>\phi(\bar{a}_0,\dots x_1, x_2)</math> be a covariant of order <math>\epsilon</math> appertaining to a quantic of order <math>n</math>,
{{block center|<math>\phi(\overline{\text{A}}_0,\dots\xi_1\xi_2)=(\lambda\mu)^w\phi(\bar{a}_0,\dots\lambda_1\xi_1+\mu_1\xi_2,\lambda_2\xi_1+\mu_2\xi_2);</math>}}
we find that the left- and right-hand sides are of degrees <math>n\theta</math> and <math>2w+\epsilon</math> respectively in <math>\lambda_1</math>, <math>\mu_1</math>, <math>\lambda_2</math>, <math>\mu_2</math>, and thence <math>n\theta=2w+\epsilon</math>.

''Symbolic Identities''.— For the purpose of manipulating symbolic expressions it is necessary to be in possession of certain simple identities which connect certain symbolic products. From the three equations
{{block center|<math>a_x=a_1x_1+a_2x_2,\ b_x=b_1x_1+b_2x_2,\ c_x=c_1x_1+c_2x_2,</math>}}
we find by eliminating <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_2</math> the relation
{{block center|<math>a_x(bc)+b_x(ca)+c_x(ab)=0</math> . . . (I.)}}
Introduce now new umbrae <math>d_1</math>, <math>d_2</math> and recall that <math>+d_2-d_1</math> are cogredient with <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_2</math>. We may in any relation substitute for any pair of quantities any other cogredient pair so that writing <math>+d_2</math>, <math>-d_1</math> for <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_2</math>, and noting that <math>g_x</math> then becomes <math>(gd)</math>, the above-written identity becomes
{{block center|<math>(ad)(bc)+(bd)(ca)+(cd)(ab)=0</math> . . . (II.)}}
Similarly in (I.), writing for <math>c_1</math>, <math>c_2</math> the cogredient pair <math>-y_2, +y_1</math>, we obtain
{{block center|<math>a_xb_y-a_yb_x=(ab)(xy).</math> . . . . . (III.)}}
Again in (I.) transposing <math>a_x(bc)</math> to the other side and squaring, we obtain
{{block center|<math>2(ac)(bc)a_xb_x=(bc)^2a^2_x+(ac)^2b_x-(ab)^2c^2_x</math> . (IV.)}}
and herein writing <math>d_2, -d_1</math> for <math>x_1</math>, <math>x_2</math>,
{{block center|<math>2(ac)(bc)(ad)(bd)=(bc)^2(ad)^2+(ac)^2(bd)^2-(ab)^2(cd)^2.</math> (V.)}}

As an illustration multiply (IV.) throughout by <math>a^{n-2}_x b^{n-2}_x c^{n-2}_x</math> so that each term may denote a covariant of an <math>n^{ic}</math>.
{{block center|<math>2(ac)(bc)a^{n-1}_x b^{n-1}_x c^{n-1}_x</math>}}
{{block center|<math>=(bc)^2a^n_xb^{n-2}_x c^{n-2}_x+(ac)^2a^{n-2}_x b^{n-2}_x c^{n-2}_x-(ab)^2a^{n-2}_x b^{n-2}_x c^n_x,</math>}}

{{smaller|<sup>1</sup> The weight of a term <math>\bar{a}^{k_0}_0\bar{a}^{k_1}_1\dots\bar{a}^{k_n}_n</math> is defined as being <math>k_1+2k_2+\dots+nk_n</math>.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
